en.title: GAO finds minimal Pentagon progress accounting for $31 billion in F-35 parts
en.summary: The US Government Accountability Office said in a report published on November 9, 2026, that the Pentagon has made "minimal progress" in accounting for F-35 parts worth about $31 billion, with incomplete records, unlogged repair parts and unresolved losses.
body: The US Department of Defense has made "minimal progress" in accounting for F-35 parts worth approximately $31 billion, according to a US Government Accountability Office (GAO) report published on November 9, 2026. As of March 2026, the program held about 26 million parts at more than 700 contractor- and government-managed facilities worldwide, serving the US military, seven partner nations and 12 foreign military sales customers. DoD officials said its total value was likely understated.

The F-35 Joint Program Office tracks the inventory through its Enterprise Logistics Management System (ELMS), which does not interface directly with the prime contractors' property management systems, and contractors submit data on the shared spares pool quarterly. In a December 2025 contractor submission, only 29% of records included serial numbers. As of March 2026, about 17,000 parts undergoing maintenance or repair, valued at approximately $1.3 billion, had not been entered into ELMS, and DoD officials said their value could reach $2.5 billion once missing costs were included. The JPO's latest physical inventory also failed to fully verify whether recorded parts existed or whether the records were complete, relying on data from a prime contractor whose property management system had received a "disapproved" rating from the Defense Contract Management Agency. The Pentagon is now working toward its first full inventory under a new audit effort, targeted for March 2027.

More than a million reported parts losses remain unresolved: in May 2023, GAO reported that one prime contractor had recorded losses involving more than one million F-35 parts, valued at over $85 million, between May 2018 and October 2022, and three years later the JPO still did not know the status of those losses. Under a one-time bulk reporting process authorized by DCMA in June 2025, the contractor submitted about $28 million in losses dating from 2012 through 2025, and DCMA found the contractor financially liable for approximately $6 million, but JPO officials could not determine whether any of the newly submitted losses overlapped with the $85 million identified in 2023. DoD accepted all four new GAO recommendations, while 26 of the 34 recommendations previously issued by GAO and the DoD Inspector General remain open. Auditors have reported an F-35-related material weakness since fiscal year 2019, and DoD has received a disclaimer of opinion in every full audit through fiscal year 2025. The JPO's Global Support Solution Reset aims to raise the mission-capable rate from 44% in fiscal year 2025 to 80% by 2030; GAO estimated in June 2026 that the plan would require about $13.7 billion in additional US funding through fiscal year 2031, including $7.3 billion for spare parts and repair materials.

facts.claim: According to a US Government Accountability Office (GAO) report published on November 9, 2026, the US Department of Defense has made "minimal progress" in accounting for F-35 parts worth approximately $31 billion.

As of March 2026, the program held about 26 million parts at more than 700 contractor- and government-managed facilities worldwide, serving the US military, seven partner nations and 12 foreign military sales customers, and DoD officials said its total value was likely understated.

The F-35 Joint Program Office tracks the inventory through its Enterprise Logistics Management System (ELMS), which does not interface directly with the prime contractors' property management systems, and contractors submit data on the shared spares pool quarterly; in a December 2025 contractor submission, only 29% included serial numbers.

As of March 2026, about 17,000 parts undergoing maintenance or repair, valued at approximately $1.3 billion, had not been entered into ELMS, and DoD officials said their value could reach $2.5 billion once missing costs were included.

The JPO's latest physical inventory failed to fully verify whether recorded parts existed or whether the records were complete, relying on data from a prime contractor whose property management system had received a "disapproved" rating from the Defense Contract Management Agency.
The Pentagon is now working toward its first full inventory under a new audit effort, targeted for March 2027.

In May 2023, GAO reported that one prime contractor had recorded losses involving more than one million F-35 parts, valued at over $85 million, between May 2018 and October 2022, and three years later the JPO still did not know the status of those losses; the latest report does not identify whether the contractor was Lockheed Martin or Pratt & Whitney.

Under a one-time bulk reporting process authorized by DCMA in June 2025, the contractor submitted about $28 million in losses dating from 2012 through 2025, and DCMA found the contractor financially liable for approximately $6 million, but JPO officials could not determine whether any of the newly submitted losses overlapped with the $85 million identified in 2023.

DoD accepted all four new GAO recommendations, covering loss monitoring, accountability procedures, training and staffing, while 26 of the 34 recommendations previously issued by GAO and the DoD Inspector General on the issue remain open.
Auditors have reported an F-35-related material weakness since fiscal year 2019, while DoD has received a disclaimer of opinion in every full audit through fiscal year 2025.

The JPO's Global Support Solution Reset aims to raise the mission-capable rate from 44% in fiscal year 2025 to 80% by 2030, and GAO estimated in June 2026 that the plan would require about $13.7 billion in additional US funding through fiscal year 2031, including $7.3 billion for spare parts and repair materials.

zh.title: 美政府問責局：五角大廈對310億美元F-35零件帳目進展甚微
zh.summary: 美國政府問責局11月9日公布報告指出，五角大廈在清點價值約310億美元F-35零件方面進展甚微；截至2026年3月，約2600萬件零件分散於700多處設施，約1萬7000件維修中零件、價值約13億美元未登錄於庫存系統。
body: 美國政府問責局11月9日公布報告指出，美國國防部在清點價值約310億美元F-35零件方面進展甚微。截至2026年3月，F-35計畫持有約2600萬件零件，分散於全球700多處承包商與政府管理設施，服務美軍、7個夥伴國家與12個對外軍售客戶；國防部官員表示，總價值可能被低估。

問題出在紀錄不全：F-35聯合計畫辦公室以企業後勤管理系統追蹤庫存，但該系統未與主承包商的財產管理系統直接介接，承包商每季才提交一次共用備件庫資料；2025年12月提交的資料中，僅29%附有零件序號。截至2026年3月，約1萬7000件正在維修或修理的零件、價值約13億美元未登錄於系統，國防部官員表示，計入缺失成本後價值可能達25億美元；最近一次實體盤點也未能完整核實零件是否存在或紀錄是否完整，且引用了一家財產管理系統遭國防合約管理局評為「disapproved」的主承包商資料。

五角大廈正推動新的稽核工作，目標2027年3月完成首次完整盤點。國防部已接受政府問責局提出的4項新建議，但政府問責局與國防部監察長先前提出的34項建議中，仍有26項未結案；審計人員自2019財政年度起即報告與F-35相關的重大缺失，國防部在截至2025財政年度的每次完整審計中均獲「無法表示意見」。此外，聯合計畫辦公室推動的全球支援方案重置計畫，目標將任務妥善率自2025財政年度的44%提升至2030年的80%，政府問責局2026年6月估計，至2031財政年度需額外137億美元美國經費，其中73億美元用於備件與修理材料。
